items.title: Ed Shaughnessy Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: would you believe that Benny Goodman had never played in Europe until he took myself and Dick Hyman who is here and Roy Eldridge and Zoot

ctx.x: But I’ll bet you were playing great time.

I’ll tell you it’s pretty good for a nineteen year old. It’s pretty good. Yeah. I mean naturally there are some things that could be improved, but I think you always feel like that. It’s a good hot band if you ever hear the record. It holds up pretty good today. We had very talented people in that band, really good people. So from there on I moved into a lot of the bigger bands. I played with Tommy Dorsey after Buddy Rich left. And I did Benny Goodman’s first European tour, which has never gotten much notice…

Sims and Toots Thielmans we picked up and an English bass player named Charlie Short, and that was Benny Goodman’s first appearance in Europe in 1950. I mean never – even at the height of his popularity. You know Louis had gone over there from like the late 20’s or early 30’s, he was the king over there. And Benny Goodman, as big as he was here, had never played in Europe. I couldn’t figure out why. And he was hugely received over there. So that was a nice all-star group to work with. items.title: Ed Shaughnessy Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: His dynamic playing and vivacious personality have sparked the bands of Jack Teagarden, Benny Goodman, Duke Ellington and George Shearing.

ctx.x: Ed Shaughnessy may be the most recognized drummer in the country. His dynamic playing and vivacious personality have sparked the bands of Jack Teagarden, Benny Goodman, Duke Ellington and George Shearing. A native of Jersey City, Ed’s first playing experience was in the clubs of the flourishing jazz scene on New York’s 52nd Street. In the 50’s he was kept busy in the studios and as a staff drummer with CBS television. As the Tonight Show drummer, Ed became a familiar face with nation-wide audiences and moved to…
Ed was interviewed in Clinton, New York on April 25, 1998 by Monk Rowe, director of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive.
